title: Breast Cancer: Molecular Biology, BRCA Mutations, Targeted Therapy and Survivorship

content.intro: Breast cancer has been described in medical texts dating back to ancient Egypt around 1600 BCE. The Greek physician Hippocrates (460-370 BCE) is credited with being the first to document breast cancer cases. In the 19th century, the Scottish surgeon John Rodman (1805-1879) reported a high incidence of breast cancer in his family, which led to the discovery of the genetic component of the disease. The American Cancer Society was founded in 1913, and since then, numerous organizations have been established to support breast cancer research and awareness.
key_points: Ancient Egyptian medical texts described breast cancer around 1600 BCE
Hippocrates documented breast cancer cases in the 5th century BCE
John Rodman reported a high incidence of breast cancer in his family in the 19th century
The American Cancer Society was founded in 1913
Landmark papers by Janet Rowley (1973) and Mary-Claire King (1990) contributed to the understanding of breast cancer genetics
The discovery of the BRCA1 gene in 1994 and the BRCA2 gene in 1995 revolutionized breast cancer research
Nobel prizes were awarded to scientists who contributed to the understanding of cancer biology, including Peyton Rous (1966) and Harold Varmus (1989)
Famous cases, such as the story of Nancy Reagan, have raised awareness about breast cancer and the importance of screening

lessons.title: Pathophysiology and Aetiology of Breast Cancer

content.intro: Breast cancer is a complex disease involving the interplay of genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors. The molecular mechanisms underlying breast cancer involve the activation of oncogenes and the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes. The most common subtypes of breast cancer are luminal A, luminal B, HER2-positive, and triple-negative. Genetic factors, such as mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, significantly increase the risk of developing breast cancer.
key_points: Breast cancer involves the activation of oncogenes and the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes
The most common subtypes of breast cancer are luminal A, luminal B, HER2-positive, and triple-negative
Genetic factors, such as mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, increase the risk of developing breast cancer
Hormonal factors, such as estrogen and progesterone, play a role in the development and progression of breast cancer
Environmental factors, such as radiation exposure and certain chemicals, may also contribute to breast cancer risk
The PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK signaling pathways are involved in breast cancer pathogenesis
Epigenetic alterations, such as DNA methylation and histone modification, also play a role in breast cancer
The tumor microenvironment, including immune cells and stromal cells, influences breast cancer progression

content.intro: Breast cancer can present with a variety of symptoms, including a palpable mass, nipple discharge, or skin changes. The cardinal symptoms of breast cancer are a painless lump or thickening in the breast, changes in breast size or shape, and nipple inversion or discharge. The stages of breast cancer range from stage 0 (ductal carcinoma in situ) to stage IV (metastatic disease). Atypical presentations, such as inflammatory breast cancer or Paget's disease of the breast, require prompt recognition and treatment.
key_points: The cardinal symptoms of breast cancer are a painless lump or thickening in the breast, changes in breast size or shape, and nipple inversion or discharge

Atypical presentations, such as inflammatory breast cancer or Paget's disease of the breast, require prompt recognition and treatment
Breast cancer can also present with systemic symptoms, such as weight loss or fatigue
The clinical presentation of breast cancer can vary depending on the subtype and stage
A thorough clinical examination, including a breast examination and axillary lymph node assessment, is essential for diagnosis
Imaging studies, such as mammography and ultrasound, are used to evaluate the extent of disease

content.intro: The diagnosis of breast cancer involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies, and pathological examination. The diagnostic criteria for breast cancer include a combination of clinical and radiological findings, as well as histopathological confirmation. Scoring systems, such as the Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS), are used to standardize the interpretation of imaging studies. Laboratory tests, such as tumor markers and genetic tests, are used to evaluate the extent of disease and guide treatment.
key_points: The diagnosis of breast cancer involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies, and pathological examination
The diagnostic criteria for breast cancer include a combination of clinical and radiological findings, as well as histopathological confirmation
Scoring systems, such as the Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS), are used to standardize the interpretation of imaging studies
Laboratory tests, such as tumor markers and genetic tests, are used to evaluate the extent of disease and guide treatment
Imaging studies, such as mammography, ultrasound, and MRI, are used to evaluate the extent of disease
Pathological examination, including biopsy and histopathological analysis, is essential for diagnosis
The diagnosis of breast cancer can be challenging, and a multidisciplinary approach is often necessary
Differential diagnoses, such as benign breast lesions or other malignancies, must be considered in the diagnostic workup

lessons.title: Treatment — Pharmacological & Non-pharmacological
key_points: Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer is treated with tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors
HER2-positive breast cancer is treated with trastuzumab or pertuzumab
Chemotherapy is used for triple-negative breast cancer
Surgery and radiation therapy are used for early-stage breast cancer
Targeted therapies such as PARP inhibitors are used for BRCA-mutated breast cancer
Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors is being explored for breast cancer treatment
Non-pharmacological treatments include lifestyle modifications and psychological support
Clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate new treatments and combination therapies
lessons.text: Breast cancer treatment has evolved significantly over the years, with a shift towards targeted therapies and personalized medicine. Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer is treated with tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors, while HER2-positive breast cancer is treated with trastuzumab or pertuzumab. Chemotherapy is used for triple-negative breast cancer, and surgery and radiation therapy are used for early-stage breast cancer. Targeted therapies such as PARP inhibitors are used for BRCA-mutated breast cancer, and immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors is being explored for breast cancer treatment. Non-pharmacological treatments include lifestyle modifications and psychological support. Clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate new treatments and combination therapies.

lessons.title: Complications & Prognosis
key_points: Breast cancer recurrence occurs in up to 30% of patients
Metastatic breast cancer has a 5-year survival rate of 27%
Lymphedema is a common complication of breast cancer treatment
Cardiac toxicity is a potential side effect of certain breast cancer treatments
Osteoporosis is a risk factor for breast cancer patients undergoing hormone therapy
Fatigue and cognitive impairment are common symptoms in breast cancer survivors
Prognostic scores such as the Nottingham Prognostic Index are used to predict patient outcomes
Genomic assays such as Oncotype DX are used to guide treatment decisions
lessons.text: Breast cancer complications and prognosis are critical aspects of patient care. Breast cancer recurrence occurs in up to 30% of patients, and metastatic breast cancer has a 5-year survival rate of 27%. Lymphedema is a common complication of breast cancer treatment, and cardiac toxicity is a potential side effect of certain breast cancer treatments. Osteoporosis is a risk factor for breast cancer patients undergoing hormone therapy, and fatigue and cognitive impairment are common symptoms in breast cancer survivors. Prognostic scores such as the Nottingham Prognostic Index are used to predict patient outcomes, and genomic assays such as Oncotype DX are used to guide treatment decisions.

lessons.title: Special Populations & Emerging Therapies
key_points: BRCA-mutated breast cancer is more common in Ashkenazi Jewish women
Triple-negative breast cancer is more common in African American women
Pregnancy-associated breast cancer is a rare but aggressive subtype
Paediatric breast cancer is extremely rare but requires specialized care
Elderly breast cancer patients may require modified treatment approaches
Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors is being explored for breast cancer treatment
CAR-T cell therapy is being investigated for metastatic breast cancer
Nanoparticle-based therapies are being developed for targeted breast cancer treatment
lessons.text: Special populations and emerging therapies are critical aspects of breast cancer care. BRCA-mutated breast cancer is more common in Ashkenazi Jewish women, and triple-negative breast cancer is more common in African American women. Pregnancy-associated breast cancer is a rare but aggressive subtype, and paediatric breast cancer is extremely rare but requires specialized care. Elderly breast cancer patients may require modified treatment approaches, and immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors is being explored for breast cancer treatment. CAR-T cell therapy is being investigated for metastatic breast cancer, and nanoparticle-based therapies are being developed for targeted breast cancer treatment.

lessons.title: Clinical Case & Applied Knowledge
key_points: A 45-year-old woman presents with a palpable breast mass and is diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma
The patient undergoes genetic testing and is found to have a BRCA1 mutation
The patient is treated with a PARP inhibitor and undergoes surgery and radiation therapy
The patient experiences fatigue and cognitive impairment during treatment
The patient requires ongoing surveillance and follow-up care to monitor for recurrence
The patient's family members are advised to undergo genetic testing and counseling
The patient's treatment plan is modified based on genomic assay results
The patient's quality of life is prioritized throughout the treatment process
